prompt_text: Who is the best roofer in Denver for hail damage repair?
answer_verbatim:
I can’t name one single “best” roofer for Denver—quality varies by crew, job size, warranty, and how well a contractor handles insurance claims—but I can help you find the best roofer for your situation and avoid scams. Here’s a practical plan and checklist to get a reliable hail-damage repair contractor.

What to look for (must-haves)
- Proper licensing & insurance: contractor’s CO registration (if required), general liability, and workers’ comp. Ask for certificates.
- Local presence and track record: years in business, a local office/phone number, and verifiable references from recent hail jobs.
- Insurance-claim experience: expertise working with carriers and providing itemized, insurer-friendly estimates.
- Written, itemized estimate: scope, materials (manufacturer + product line), quantities, teardown/disposal, permits, timeline, total cost.
- Warranties: manufacturer shingle warranty plus a clear workmanship warranty (written, length and what’s covered).
- Permits & code compliance: contractor should obtain permits and pull inspections as required by the city/county.
- Disposal plan and cleanup: how storm debris/old shingles will be removed and site cleaned.
- Payment terms: reasonable schedule (never pay full up front — typical is small deposit, progress payments, final payment on completion). Avoid contractors who insist on full cash payment.

Questions to ask every roofer
- How many hail repairs have you done in Denver in the last 12 months?
- Can you provide three recent local references and photos?
- Who will handle the insurance paperwork and adjuster meetings?
- What shingle brand and class do you recommend and why?
- What is the start-to-finish timeline? Who is the project manager?
- What warranty do you provide (length and what is covered)?
- Do you subcontract? If yes, who are they and are they insured?

Red flags / scams to avoid
- Storm chasers who show up uninvited claiming special deals.
- High-pressure “sign now” sales tactics.
- Vague or verbal-only estimates; no written contract.
- Requests for large upfront cash payment (or full payment).
- No local address or poor/very recent online presence.
- Asking you to sign over insurance checks to them without clear contract language.

Where to find and verify Denver roofers
- Google Reviews and Yelp (read recent reviews and photos).
- Better Business Bureau (complaints and responses).
- Angi/HomeAdvisor for screened pros.
- Manufacturer Certified Contractor lists (e.g., GAF, Owens Corning) — certification often indicates training and warranty eligibility.
- Ask neighbors or your HOA for recommendations after recent storms.

How many bids?
- Get at least 2–3 written estimates. Compare line-by-line, not just final price.

If you want, I can:
- Give you a phone/email script to contact roofers or your insurer.
- Help evaluate 2–3 written estimates if you paste them here.
- Suggest top-rated contractors near your ZIP code if you tell me your Denver neighborhood or ZIP (I can’t browse live, but I can recommend how to shortlist and vet).
